item.title: Designing Collaborative Virtual Environments for Software Engineering Education
item.description: arXiv:2611.14578v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Collaborative virtual environments offer opportunities to make software models available for shared inspection, but educational design and usability need to be examined separately from claims of learning effectiveness. This article presents MetaSEE, an approach connecting requirements guidance, a Web XR feature model, a reusable UML component, and a browser-based multiuser platform. We synthesize documented formative evaluations of the framework (16 participations), feature model (15), UML component (9), and platform (14). These counts represent evaluation participations; the same 12 developers took part in the first two evaluations. The principal platform study involved six teachers working individually and eight students working in four pairs through desktop or notebook computers, keyboard, and mouse. The documentary synthesis traces educational intentions to implemented features and reported difficulties. Participants identified potential value in shared modeling and simulation, alongside navigation, interaction, visualization, and distraction concerns. A numerical audit reconstructs a student System Usability Scale mean of 67.50 from published item frequencies, conflicting with the reported 79.38; an incomplete teacher item distribution prevents recovery of that group's overall mean. The contribution is a traceable account of educational design and formative limitations, with practical implications for onboarding, model readability, collaboration, and evaluation reporting. The evidence supports bounded feasibility and perceived usefulness, without establishing learning gains, sustained engagement, or adoption.
item.dc:creator: Filipe Fernandes, Cl\'audia Werner

item.title: When Evaluators of AI Agents Disagree: An Empirical Study of Native Scoring, LLM Judges, and Commit-Boundary Checks on tau2-bench
item.description: arXiv:2611.14581v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic workflows, in which a large language model (LLM) calls tools to read and write data, are evaluated in two ways. Benchmarks compare the final state against a gold answer. Deployed services have none; an LLM judge reads the transcript and decides. Practice treats the two as interchangeable. This paper measures whether they are. We ran 2,160 episodes in tau2-bench's airline and retail domains and recorded every database write. We scored each episode four ways: native scoring against gold state, an LLM judge, that judge given the policy document, and the boundary evaluator, a minimal rule-based check of whether a write was expected against whether one occurred in the trace. Two annotators independently labeled 120 episodes for task correctness, policy compliance, and commitment correctness. The judge repeated its verdict 98.2% of the time but agreed with native scoring on 56.2%. In 11 episodes the agent executed a forbidden write. The judge passed 10 to 11, with or without the policy or transcript. A stronger judge still passed 6. The boundary evaluator, with no model call, caught all 11; no judge significantly exceeded it on human labels. Forbidden writes occurred in 11.1% of episodes without gates. Verification, correction, and safe-termination gates did not reduce them significantly. The traces show a candidate cause: the gates' evidence digest dropped the order status and customer authentication, so valid requests were rejected. The choice of evaluator decides the conclusion; the minimal check exposes failures the judges miss. Traces, code, prompts, and labels are released.
item.dc:creator: Sungbin Im

item.title: Discovering the Relation Between Architectural Models and Reference Architectures
item.description: arXiv:2611.14606v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Assessing whether concrete software architectures are consistent with their reference architecture (RA) is essential to ensure that architectural decisions scale coherently across projects, preserving the quality attributes the RA was designed to guarantee. In the absence of dedicated techniques, mapping the components of an architectural model onto a predefined RA can be addressed only with general-purpose model-comparison algorithms. Our experiments show that these algorithms are inaccurate when applied to RAs. To address this gap, we propose Reference Architecture Mapping Discovery (RAMD), an LLM-based workflow that combines model analysis with structured prompting, and refines results through an iterative RA compliance-checking mechanism. We evaluate RAMD on 64 open-source architectural models spanning three RAs from the IoT, self-driving, and smart parking domains. With domain knowledge and GPT-4o, RAMD reaches 85.8% mapping accuracy and outperforms the strongest baseline by 44.6 percentage points, while ensuring structural consistency with the RA.
item.dc:creator: Thi Dinh Tran, Maria Teresa Rossi, Ludovico Iovino, Leonardo Mariani

item.title: Outcome Over Learning? Evidence from Student Use of AI Code Assistants for Unit Test Writing
item.description: arXiv:2611.14664v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) code assistants are rapidly being adopted in programming education, yet little is known about how students naturally use these tools when given unrestricted access. In a user study investigating AI-assisted unit test writing, we observed that a majority of students adopted a one-shot interaction strategy, asking the AI to generate a complete unit test directly from the initial requirements. While this approach is capable of efficiently producing a solution, it shifts students' focus from learning how to write effective unit tests to simply completing the task. Moreover, because students rarely engaged in critically evaluating, refining, or iterating on AI-generated output, they may be missing opportunities to develop the critical thinking skills that are essential for effective and responsible use of AI. In an effort to shift student focus from outcome to learning we also discuss how training, accountability and improved learning task design can better support a more learning-centric responsible use of AI.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Hinbest, Jeremy S. Bradbury, Michael A. Miljanovic

item.title: Where Should the Code Go? Locating Foundation-Model Errors in Bitemporal Inventory Simulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.14671v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Operational reports carry two clocks: when an event happened and when its report arrived; later reports can revise earlier ones. A foundation-model component that maintains the state supported by the reports visible at a cutoff, then rolls a supplied scenario forward, can be helped by exact code before it, after it or inside the call, or asked to reason harder. We ask which remedy removes which error, for which models, on an exactly solvable lost-sales inventory environment: 36,672 independently rescored requests over twelve configurations of closed and open-weight models, with a forced-answer-call interface as a control and protocols frozen before the calls. Weak models fail in separable ways. Canonical input removes report-selection error, exact continuation removes rollout error, neither repairs the other, and which error dominates differs by model; strong models are at ceiling on raw reports. Asking for more reasoning is no substitute and can depend on the interface: under a forced answer call high effort collapses GPT-5.4 mini and DeepSeek V4 Pro, which gain or hold under automatic choice; on its provider the forced call disables reasoning for DeepSeek V4 Flash; and at high effort gpt-oss exhausts its output budget. The contribution is a controlled component diagnostic, released with every request, and evidence that for some model and provider pairs the tool-calling interface confounds reasoning evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Durga Sandeep Saluru, Lanchen Song, Aditya Kumaran

item.title: Mach2: Scientific Discovery Platform with Deterministic Execution Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2611.14777v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language-model agents can formulate workflows and invoke specialized tools, yet compliance with natural-language operating rules is not guaranteed by prompting alone. Mach2 addresses this limitation by coupling Eigen orchestration to deterministic, lint-like checks of tool requests, source changes, acceptance tests, and artifact contracts. Domain requirements are represented as executable predicates: mandatory failures prevent advancement of the checked operation, while diagnostic findings are retained for correction or review. User-specified test-driven development (TDD), CodeGrapher's abstract-syntax-tree analysis, and history-guided evolutionary search provide complementary verification and optimization mechanisms. Mach2 also generates task-specific agent packages for execution through independently selected endpoints. The originating harness validates returned artifacts against declared interfaces and evidence requirements without assuming continuous supervision of the remote run. Model-internal-knowledge (MIK) dependencies are recorded separately from source-grounded and test-supported findings. This paper formalizes the rule-gated execution model and the agent-package lifecycle, and proposes measurable criteria for evaluating rule compliance, engineering validity, and cross-endpoint task continuity.
item.dc:creator: Vansh Sharma, Venkat Raman

item.title: Typify: A Tool for Usage-driven Type Inference in Python
item.description: arXiv:2611.14879v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Python's dynamic type system, while expressive and flexible, creates significant challenges for static analysis tools in unannotated or partially annotated codebases. Existing approaches either require pre-existing type annotations, or depend on deep learning models that demand large training corpora and significant computational resources. We present Typify, a lightweight, usage-driven static type inference engine that infers precise type information across entire Python projects without annotations or training data. Typify integrates symbolic execution, fixpoint analysis, and context-matching retrieval to propagate types across modules, functions, and recursive call structures. The tool is available as both a command-line interface (CLI) for batch inference, evaluation and downstream integration with other tools, and a Visual Studio Code (VS Code) extension for interactive type assistance. Evaluation on the ManyTypes4Py and Typilus datasets shows that Typify outperforms all static baselines and closely matches state-of-the-art hybrid deep learning approaches, while running approximately 10x faster.
item.dc:creator: Hassan Aman, Ali Aman, Muhammad Asaduzzaman, Shaowei Wang, Jessica Chen

item.title: Caprese: Change Impact Recommendation Using History and Runtime Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.14937v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Change impact recommendation identifies program entities potentially affected by source code changes. Historical co-changes and runtime dependencies provide complementary evidence, particularly in JavaScript, where dynamic and asynchronous behaviour complicates dependency analysis. We present Caprese, an open-source framework for function-level change impact recommendation in Node.js. Given a change set, it produces a ranked impact set of potentially affected functions. It supports repository-based recommendation through confidence-guided mining of recurring, change-set-relevant co-change patterns of varying lengths; dynamic recommendation through execution-derived dependencies involving calls, callbacks, events, timers, and shared state; and hybrid recommendation integrating both analyses. Its modular implementation supports reusable analyses. Evaluation on ten open-source applications and 100 selected change sets shows that, on average across projects, 77.4% of the relevant functions among the top 60 hybrid recommendations are identified exclusively by one analysis, demonstrating substantial complementarity. Dynamic recommendation achieves the highest mean precision among the top five recommendations (0.65), while repository-based recommendation performs best when the ranking is extended to 60 recommendations (0.42). Hybrid recommendation outperforms TARMAQ on average but does not consistently outperform the individual modes. Caprese is publicly available with source code, documentation, and evaluation artifacts.
item.dc:creator: Sadjad Tavakoli, Saba Alimadadi

item.title: TSBugs Explorer: Exploring and Benchmarking TypeScript Bugs
item.description: arXiv:2611.14940v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Curated datasets of real-world software bugs support empirical research in software testing, debugging, and automated program repair. However, exploring heterogeneous bug collections, comparing fault characteristics across projects, and constructing research-specific subsets often require manual inspection and custom scripts. We present TSBugs Explorer, an interactive visual analytics platform built upon our previously-published dataset of 633 bugs from 16 open-source TypeScript repositories, classified into 11 fault categories. The platform integrates bug records, repository characteristics, dependency information, and taxonomy guidance through coordinated visualizations, interactive filtering, and detailed bug inspection. It supports alternative aggregation and normalization of fault distributions, pairwise repository comparisons, and analysis of differences in observed fault profiles. An integrated benchmark builder allows researchers to select bug subsets using multiple criteria, inspect their composition, and export records in CSV or JSON format. We demonstrate the platform through three research workflows: fault characterization, cross-repository comparison, and task-specific benchmark construction. Functional validation by two authors confirmed selection correctness, visualization consistency, export integrity, and reproducibility across the tested workflows. By making the existing corpus easier to explore, compare, and reuse, TSBugs Explorer facilitates systematic, research-specific selection and export of TypeScript bug records.
item.dc:creator: TianYi Tang, Saba Alimadadi

item.title: LOHRE: Execution-Grounded Type Recovery via LLM-Orchestrated Hybrid Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.14946v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Documenting stripped binary functions for security analysis requires recovering function interfaces and user-defined type (UDT) layouts from machine code. Existing large language model (LLM)-based methods face two limitations: they lack execution-based validation to detect inferred UDTs inconsistent with actual memory layouts, and may overlook evidence about shared UDTs across functions without direct call relationships. We present LLM-Orchestrated Hybrid Reverse Engineering (LOHRE), a framework that treats inferred UDTs as falsifiable hypotheses and tests them against program execution. LOHRE uses a hypothesize-validate-refine loop to test candidate layouts through paired dynamic slice emulation of baseline and mutated inputs. To reduce the cost of processing lengthy execution histories, the Execution-Depth Heuristic (EDH) compresses paired traces into an execution-depth difference and a summary of the tested field's observed uses. A cross-function knowledge base aggregates compatible UDT hypotheses and field-level confidence scores to guide testing and hypothesis refinement. We evaluate LOHRE on RealType at four optimization levels and a Windows remote procedure call (RPC) dataset. LOHRE achieves an average UDT Structural accuracy of 57.85% across RealType's four optimization levels and 35.6% on Windows RPC, outperforming the evaluated static baselines. Disabling dynamic validation reduces accuracy to 19.28% on RealType and 9.2% on Windows RPC. Removing the cross-function knowledge base reduces accuracy to 41.03% on RealType and 10.0% on Windows RPC. Replacing EDH's compressed feedback with full execution traces reduces recovery accuracy while increasing token use by 3.7 times and runtime by 3.0 times. These results indicate that execution-based validation, compact feedback, and cross-function evidence contribute to accurate and efficient UDT recovery.
item.dc:creator: Hao Jiang, Yujie Yang, Tao Li, Chenhui Cui, Liangfeng Xu, Chengjie Liu, Weiping Wen, Rubing Huang, Tsong Yueh Chen

item.title: JoyFrontBench: Evaluating Front-End Coding Agents through Goal-Oriented Acceptance Contracts
item.description: arXiv:2611.14952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Front-end coding agents are expected to produce applications that fulfill user goals, yet high task scores can coexist with failures in essential workflows. Evaluating these agents therefore requires an explicit distinction between partial implementation and application success. We introduce JoyFrontBench, a benchmark that makes this distinction through goal-oriented acceptance contracts. Each contract identifies core tasks and mandatory criteria before generation: a core task passes only when all mandatory criteria are satisfied and a shared completion threshold is met, while application success requires every core task to pass on the same operational artifact within a single run. Derived from practitioner requirements, JoyFrontBench comprises 100 front-end development problems, 764 tasks, and 2,596 atomic criteria, with reviewed annotations linking user goals to core tasks and evidence requirements. The evaluation framework combines evidence-grounded judgments with deterministic record auditing and fixed scoring rules, preserving graded task assessment alongside explicit core-task and application-level acceptance. We evaluate five coding models under two agent harnesses, OpenHands and OpenCode, on the 70-problem test set; the remaining 30 problems form a public set for validation and diagnostic analyses. Under OpenHands, the mean Average Task Score (ATS) across models is 87.69%, while the mean Application Success Rate (ASR) is 51.52%. Further analyses reveal changes in model rankings across harnesses and variation in application success across repeated runs. These findings highlight the limitations of aggregate task scores in characterizing application success and motivate explicit assessment of core-goal fulfillment alongside graded task performance.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyi Qiao, Yicheng Wang, Jianan Lin, Xiaoyang Ji, Dongyi Lv, Yidan Huang, Shi Suo, Shiying Fan, Nan Duan, Jiaqi Wang

item.title: FIRE: Failure Isolation and Reliability for Production-Connected Experiments at Scale
item.description: arXiv:2611.14962v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pre-production changes are usually tested in isolated environments to prevent their side effects from reaching production. Some record-and-replay platforms allow a production-connected mode: candidate changes receive recorded production requests while selected downstream calls reach production dependencies. This improves fidelity before deployment, but it also introduces reliability risks. At hyperscale, experimental traffic can fan out across shared services, trigger latent defects, or send malformed input to systems serving user requests. In this paper, we show how production-connected experimentation can operate reliably in a large-scale recommendation serving system. To contain downstream effects without sacrificing realistic dependency behavior, the platform uses three complementary guardrails. Isolated tiers redirect replay traffic away from shared dependencies where replication is practical. Dependency monitors observe downstream health and experiment-attributed errors and terminate experiments after sustained violations. Traffic pinning limits experimental calls to a designated subset of downstream workers when full replication would require scarce capacity. Isolated ranking tiers process billions of replayed requests per day using under 1% of the corresponding serving capacity. Over 90 days, these tiers experienced more than 200,000 abnormal worker exits without directly affecting production-serving workers. During a separate three-month window, dependency monitors cancelled approximately 5% of experiments for the measured ranking service and accounted for 87% of its cancellations. Dependency-aware triggering also reduced code-review experiment executions by 25%. These results show that high-fidelity, production-connected experimentation can operate at scale when downstream effects are isolated where possible, bounded where necessary, and continuously monitored and attributed.
item.dc:creator: Shripad Nadgowda, Gaurav Mitra, Sing Sing Ma, Vipul Chaskar, Pradipta Ghosh, Canturk Isci, Onkar Deshpande, Edgardo Aviles-Lopez, Ryan Feng, J\'an Ondru\v{s}ek

item.title: GHA-SmellFix: Taking Action with Agentic LLMs for Detecting and Refactoring GitHub Actions Workflow Smells
item.description: arXiv:2611.14963v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continuous integration and continuous delivery workflows are key artifacts in software projects. In GitHub Actions, they encode build, test, release, deployment, and security automation in YAML. These workflows contain configuration smells affecting security, reliability, maintainability, or operational stability. Existing approaches are mostly rule-based, with rules hard to create and evolve, and typically report findings without fixes. Agentic LLM pipelines can combine contextual detection, transformation selection, and patch generation. Specialized agents can gate refactoring on positive detection verdicts, potentially avoiding unnecessary changes, but it is unclear whether decomposition improves effectiveness or mainly changes overhead. We present GHA-SmellFix, an agentic LLM pipeline for detecting and refactoring GitHub Actions workflow smells. We compare two designs: Joint, where one agent detects and refactors, and Decomposed, where separate agents detect and then refactor. We operationalize 19 smells from an existing catalog with explicit detection criteria, refactoring expectations, exclusion rules, and safety checks, and curate a ground truth of 1,710 (workflow, smell) pairs. We evaluate the designs with four LLMs (GPT-5.4-nano, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Claude Haiku 4.5, and DeepSeek V4 Flash) on 570 sampled pairs. Results show that decomposition does not universally improve patch quality; its main benefit is controlling when patch generation is attempted. It helps models prone to missing smells and can reduce overhead by gating patches. Once a smell is correctly detected, clean refactoring is generally effective, making detection the main end-to-end bottleneck. However, false positives can trigger unnecessary edits to execution-relevant constructs. Practical CI/CD agents thus need reliable abstention and construct-aware validation alongside patch generation.
item.dc:creator: Anderson Uch\^oa, Jhefferson Souza, Emanuel \'Avila, Gabriel Silva, Kevin Lira, Hui Sun, Nelson Ara\'ujo, Arthur Cordeiro, Rohit Gheyi, Wesley Assun\c{c}\~ao

item.title: Understanding Suggested Edits in Stack Overflow: A Large-Scale Empirical Study and Review Prioritization Framework
item.description: arXiv:2611.15001v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Suggested edits allow low-reputation users to improve Stack Overflow posts and contribute to the platform's knowledge base. However, we still know little about why these edits are accepted or rejected and how reviewers can efficiently identify problematic edits. In this study, we analyze 3,888,805 suggested edits submitted between 2011 and May 2023. First, we compare accepted and rejected edits using 35 features. We find significant differences between them, with the largest differences related to users' editing history. Second, we manually analyze rejected edits and identify 17 fine-grained rejection reasons. These reasons provide a more detailed understanding of why edits are rejected than Stack Overflow's predefined rejection reasons. Third, we evaluate three models for prioritizing edits based on their likelihood of rejection. The Feature Model, built using the 35 studied features, provides the best trade-off between review rate and rejected-edit recall. At a decision threshold of $\tau = 0.40$, it prioritizes 52.3% of edits for human review while capturing 80.8% of rejected edits. In comparison, the Embedding Model captures 78.8% of rejected edits while prioritizing 60.9% of edits, and the EditEx Model captures 72.5% while prioritizing 59.0%. We also conduct a complementary zero-shot evaluation on a separate set of 500 edits. The Feature Model achieves 78.0% recall at $\tau = 0.40$, compared with 23.6%-31.2% for GPT-4o, Qwen2.5-32B, and Llama-3.3-70B. Overall, our findings provide a detailed understanding of suggested-edit rejection and show that rejection-risk prediction can help prioritize potentially problematic edits for human review.
item.dc:creator: Mehedi Hasan Shanto, Muhammad Asaduzzaman, Md. Ahasanuzzaman, Alioune Ngom

item.title: Structure-Aware Quantum Circuit Equivalence Checking via Sparse Pauli Propagation
item.description: arXiv:2611.15080v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum circuit equivalence checking is essential for validating compiler optimizations, but its computational cost can vary substantially with circuit structure. We present a structure-aware equivalence checker for unitary quantum circuits based on sparse Pauli propagation. It combines two complementary verification strategies: generator propagation compares the conjugation actions of the circuits on Pauli generators, while Cut-Miter exploits cancellation between circuit products at selected cut points. A structure-aware verification procedure uses circuit characteristics to select between these strategies while explicitly accounting for numerical and approximation errors. We evaluate our framework against three existing equivalence checkers on two benchmark suites containing circuit pairs with up to 512 qubits. Across 434 scored circuit pairs, our framework produces reference-consistent decisions for 96.3% of the pairs without any incorrect verdicts, while the evaluated baselines achieve at most 68.7% reference-consistent decisions. It also achieves the lowest aggregate runtime among the evaluated tools, reducing total runtime by 48.5%--76.0% relative to these baselines. Ablation studies confirm the benefits of cut-based verification, Pauli-term pruning, and bounded propagation attempts. These results indicate that structure-aware sparse Pauli propagation, combined with complementary verification strategies and explicit error accounting, can provide an effective approach to practical quantum circuit equivalence checking.
item.dc:creator: Shangzhou Xia, Junjie Luo, Qichen Wang, Yasunari Suzuki, Jianjun Zhao

item.title: An Empirical Study of Maintainer-Identified AI Slop Pull Requests in Free and Open Source Software Projects
item.description: arXiv:2611.15159v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The FOSS ecosystem has always relied on outside contributions, notably through issues or Pull Requests (PRs), to sustain itself. With the advance of GenAI, the barrier to contributing to FOSS projects has never been lower, leading to the emergence of AI slop PRs: low-quality, low-value generated PRs. Past studies have examined AI slop PRs through theoretical, platform-level, or practitioner-account frames, but not at the project level. To this end, this study investigates the incidence of maintainer-identified AI slop PRs in FOSS projects by focusing on PRs flagged as slop by maintainers. Using a mixed-methods approach, we trace the origins of maintainer-identified AI slop PRs, quantify their volume in FOSS projects, describe their characteristics, and highlight maintainers' reasons for flagging or closing them. Our results show that the volume of maintainer-identified AI slop PRs increased in mid-2025, peaking in May 2026. These PRs are mostly additive, rarely merged, and typically closed within 3 days. The authors of these PRs disclosed the use of AI in 14% of cases, with 1% disclosing after a maintainer's request. Most PRs are closed or marked as slop without any reason provided by the maintainer. Based on our open coding, reasons range from concrete elements, like build failures, to ideological or intuitive (i.e., "looks AI to me"). This exploratory study captures a phenomenon in its early stage and highlights GenAI's potential impact on FOSS, emphasizing the pressure it puts on maintainers and the need to shift current open-source development practices.
item.dc:creator: Hugo Raskin, Xavier Devroey, Beno\^it Vanderose

item.title: Pre-QED: Environment Specifications for Agentic Verification
item.description: arXiv:2611.15207v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents are making formal verification practical at scale. Recently, many attempts have raised this as an enticing possibility. However, formal verification at scale is only meaningful if deep formal specifications capturing functionality are available for checking. Unfortunately, recent works seek to bypass this issue by using shallow specifications devised for purposes other than verification. OSS-Verify from Anthropic and Theorem, for example, reuses the fuzz harnesses of open-source libraries as specifications and has an agent prove that each harness never crashes. However, a fuzz harness follows a single sequence of API calls under a single calling context, so the resulting proof covers one usage scenario rather than the library. We argue that the bottleneck of agentic verification has shifted from how to prove to what to prove. Before zooming into verification at scale, we need deep environment specifications to prove, which is why we call our effort Pre-QED. We propose verification harnesses, executable harnesses that model all legal usages of an API, so that a proof about the harness is a proof about every well-behaved client. To construct them, we use an agentic workflow that extracts the API's usage contract from code / documentation, and uses Linear-time Temporal Logic (LTL) to rule out illegal call orders. We identify the challenges in proving verification harnesses and release our harnesses open-source as challenges for the community. The overarching vision is that verifying an open-source library should become as routine as fuzzing it, with a guarantee that covers every well-behaved client rather than a single scenario like a fuzzing harness.
item.dc:creator: Tristan Lim, Haoxin Tu, Mehtab Zafar, Zhengxiong Luo, Abhik Roychoudhury

item.title: Technical Debt Risks in AI-Assisted Software Development: Insights from Practitioners
item.description: arXiv:2611.15310v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI coding assistants increasingly support software development, raising concerns about technical debt associated with AI-generated code and development practices. We investigate these concerns through a sequential mixed-methods study involving 137 survey respondents and 20 follow-up interviews with software professionals in Bangladesh. Drawing on ten established technical debt dimensions, we examine perceived risks, contributing circumstances, maintenance consequences, validation practices, and developer understanding. Respondents expressed the strongest concerns about People Debt (73.0\%), Management Debt (70.1\%), and Architecture Debt (68.6\%), suggesting that risks extend beyond code quality. Participants associated ambiguous requirements, insufficient project context, and unrequested AI-generated changes with architectural inconsistencies, rework, and maintenance difficulties. Their experiences revealed contrasting outcomes: AI assistance supported refactoring, maintainability improvements, and testing, but also introduced rework and context misalignment. Although 89.8\% reported regularly verifying AI-generated code, participants expressed concerns about AI dependence, reduced code understanding, and review effort. They also emphasized the need for stronger architectural awareness, requirements clarification, and validation support in coding assistants. Our findings suggest that managing technical debt risks requires attention to project context, implementation decisions, and developer understanding alongside generated code quality.
item.dc:creator: Nazia Jahan, Nafisa Alam, Sourov Debnath, Arafat Rahman, S. M. Waesh Ahmed, Md Farhad Alam Bhuiyan, Mia Mohammad Imran

item.title: AgentTorrent: A Dataset of Context and Harness Engineering Artifacts on GitHub
item.description: arXiv:2611.15436v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Over the past months, developers have moved from formulating detailed prompts to engineering the context that agentic coding tools read and to configuring the underlying harnesses. For example, developers commit context files, skills, hooks, and MCP configurations to their repositories, and these files control which instructions a harness reads and which actions it can take. Developers may also commit the specs, plans, and task files that agentic coding tools and spec-driven development frameworks write for agents to implement. The AgentTorrent dataset records these files for six proprietary and open-source agentic coding tools in 10,944 engineered software projects on GitHub. It contains 62,374 configuration artifacts, the files that these artifacts import, 27,593 agentic planning documents, and more than 1.2 million commits that credit an AI tool. All heuristics used for data collection are grounded in tool documentation or derived from GitHub repositories, and we evaluate their detection accuracy with each collection. We use open-weight models to classify whether GitHub repositories host engineered software projects. Unlike most datasets, AgentTorrent links configuration artifacts, imported files, agentic planning documents, and commits that credit an AI tool within the same repositories. Configuration artifacts, planning documents, and credited commits occur together in 388 repositories. For example, our dataset allows researchers to study whether a tool is credited in commits that add instructions for that same tool and how instruction files import and contradict each other. Our data collection pipeline supports regular updates and automatically checks vendor documentation and reports unknown artifacts and agentic coding tools. The dataset and the pipeline are open-source and are archived on Zenodo.
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Baltes, Seyedmoein Mohsenimofidi, Levi B\"ohme, Vahram Nersesyan, Muhammad Auwal Abubakar, Jai Lal Lulla, Matthias Galster, Christoph Treude

item.title: KernelMutate: Mutation-Guided Validation of Generated GPU Kernels
item.description: arXiv:2611.15441v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generated GPU implementations are commonly accepted after a few differential tests, although replacement obligations may remain unchecked. We present KernelMutate, an empirical study of validation reliability using controlled faults, released implementations, and replacement tests. A five-draw anchor accepts 548 of 838 CUDA candidates. The full suite finds native FP32 witnesses for 136 accepted candidates and dtype-only findings for another 362, mostly low-precision execution limitations without established publisher guarantees. Source-guided testing identifies the full suite's 692 candidates at 26.1% lower charged cost, but yields only dtype evidence for 16 accepted candidates with native witnesses in the full suite. Independently observed context and boundary findings cover the same candidate set. Task-held-out template matching reveals differences in ranking and observation coverage: global top-eight recommendations match more probes than class-conditioned lists (51 versus 48 of 75), while conditional analyses restrict the apparent advantage at smaller limits. These template-matching results are offline measurements, not deployed-suite gains. Independent controls and replacement cases expose numerical-policy, binding, and custom-execution boundaries. Validation therefore needs to report witness domains and observation coverage alongside candidate yield and cost.
item.dc:creator: Ziyuan Li, Zihe Song, Shuxiao Xie, Mingfang Ji, Xiaofang Qi, Wei Yang, Tao Xie

item.title: KernelAudit: Contract-Aware Auditing of Validators for LLM-Generated GPU Kernels
item.description: arXiv:2611.15506v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The effectiveness of generating GPU kernels driven by a large language model (LLM) is highly dependent on the quality of the used validator (used to accept or reject a generated kernel candidate against the contracts of the given kernel-generation task), whose results inform reward assignment, candidate selection, and speedup claims during kernel generation. However, an existing validator suffers from various limitations, e.g., wrongly accepting a candidate due to missing its forbidden library use or wrongly rejecting a candidate due to determining its permitted library use as forbidden (constraints on library uses are stated in the task contracts). To assess the quality of a validator against the given task contracts, we propose an independent-audit approach for the validator by (1) construction of audit oracle: labeling a candidate as PASS or FAIL based on three separate dimensions in our proposed contract model (i.e., semantic correctness, implementation integrity, and measurement integrity) and (2) auditing of the validator against the audit oracle: comparing the labels of the candidate against the validation results produced by the validator. For semantic correctness, reference-calibrated stress tests check output correctness on valid inputs for a candidate. For implementation integrity, reference and candidate execution traces are used to determine specific library uses. For measurement integrity, timing checks assess whether the reported runtime reflects the full time needed to complete the candidate's computation. We apply our approach to assess the quality of six validators and 716 candidates from seven corpora, including constructed controls. The evaluation results show that our approach helps assess the existing six validators to have nontrivial false-reject rates. There is high-degree agreement between the candidate labels produced by our audit oracle and human judgments.
item.dc:creator: Ziyuan Li, Zihe Song, Xiaofang Qi, Wei Yang, Tao Xie

item.title: Git2KG: Mining socio-technical relationships in GitHub repositories as temporal knowledge graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.15509v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The widespread use of Git and GitHub in open source software (OSS) projects has produced large volumes of data on collaborative software development. Existing approaches to mine those data often use graph models to (i) capture communication between developers in the issue tracker, or (ii) represent developer-developer co-authorship or developer-file code ownership networks from the editing history of code artifacts. Integrating these data in a single knowledge graph (KG) is complicated by the need to disambiguate authors and match entities from multiple sources. Moreover, most works using network analysis have taken a time-aggregated perspective that neglects temporal dynamics of collaborations. To address these issues, we present Git2KG, an extensible Python library that mines temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) from GitHub repositories. Git2KG extracts fine-grained co-editing relations and code ownership from the Git log. It further disambiguates developer identities to align the resulting graphs with management and communication networks extracted from GitHub issue trackers. Git2KG supports temporal analysis by slicing development events into fixed-size, non-overlapping time windows, yielding a series of knowledge graph snapshots per repository. It further supports computing node features and labels for downstream machine learning tasks. Snapshots can then be exported to PyTorch Geometric, PathPyG, and NetworkX for temporal network analysis, visualization, and graph learning.
item.dc:creator: Lennart Hessenauer, Lisi Qarkaxhija, Ingo Scholtes

item.title: GHAgentCI: A Dataset of Coding-Agent Invocations in CI Workflow Histories
item.description: arXiv:2611.15522v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents are increasingly integrated into GitHub Actions to review pull requests, triage issues and modify code. Identifying these integrations is challenging because agentic workflows often resemble ordinary CI files, with evidence appearing in action references, shell commands and workflow conventions. We present GHAgentCI, a dataset of 15K+ workflow histories from 6K+ of 196K+ mined GitHub repositories, comprising 159K+ revisions and 205K+ agent-evidence records linked to workflow triggers and declared execution constraints. Our open-source extractor, cai-miner, detects agent-related evidence using an extensible catalogue. Manual validation of 576 stratified records confirmed 96.1% of dedicated-action matches and 98.8% of GitHub Agentic Workflow matches, with lower rates for other evidence kinds. Exploratory analyses reveal a shift toward command-line and GitHub Agentic Workflow integrations, differences in declared safeguards, and frequent removal of detected agentic workflows. GHAgentCI supports longitudinal studies of coding-agent integration into CI.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Ogenrwot, Jorge Gonzalo Delgado Cervantes, Woojoong Kim, John Businge

item.title: Testing Conversation Preservation Across LLM APIs: A Rule-Based Oracle for Detecting Silent Information Loss
item.description: arXiv:2611.15543v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM applications increasingly rely on translators and compatibility layers to move conversations across APIs. Yet a translated request can be accepted by the target API while silently losing information about instruction roles, tool interactions, error states, or generation controls. We introduce isloss, a deterministic oracle for testing conversation-information preservation across LLM API translations. It maps source and translated requests and replies to a shared intermediate representation, ConvIR, and applies explicit rules to distinguish legitimate representation changes from information loss. Unlike schema validation or reference-based differential testing, isloss requires neither a reference translation nor additional model calls. It also distinguishes avoidable loss from degradation caused by target API limitations. We evaluate isloss using specification-based fault injection, human review, and experiments on translators, gateways, and client libraries. On held-out tests, it detects 95/125 planted faults (76.0%) with 2/100 false alarms (2.0%). Across a synthetic request suite spanning six configurations of five translator codebases, 127/685 completed translations (18.5%) pass static target checks while silently changing prompt, role, or tool information in ways the target API could have preserved. In translated replies, 203/558 streams (36.4%) cause exceptions or silent corruption in at least one tested official OpenAI SDK. Targeted experiments across six models show that translation-induced changes can alter model behaviour when tasks depend on the affected information. These results establish conversation preservation as a distinct correctness requirement for reliable LLM interoperability, agent execution, and model evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Xin Liu, Xu Han, Yuxin Wang, Haoran Song, Mingjian Zhao, Lei Wang

item.title: DafnyCert: Certifying Specification Strength in Dafny
item.description: arXiv:2611.15548v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Formally verifying a method with Dafny guarantees correctness relative to its specification. However, a specification may be too permissive, allowing multiple outputs for the same input, even when the implementation produces only one. In this paper, we propose checkable certificates that provide independently verifiable evidence of whether a specification is weak or strong. A certificate of weakness contains an alternative implementation that verifies against the original specification, together with a witness input on which the original and alternative implementations produce different results. A certificate of strength is produced by constructing a harness around the original method such that successfully verifying the harness guarantees that the specification allows at most one possible output for any given input. We present DafnyCert, a tool that automatically produces these certificates. Strength is established by constructing and verifying the harness. Weakness is demonstrated by using the MutDafny mutation tool to find mutants that verify against the original specification, and by using the Hypothesis property-based testing framework to generate inputs that produce different outputs for the original program and the mutant. The resulting mutant and witness form a recheckable certificate of weakness. On a dataset of 3,910 verified Dafny methods from Dafny-Synthesis and VeriEquivBench, DafnyCert automatically certifies 3,570 methods (91.3%). We also provide certificates for the remaining 340 methods. To our knowledge, this is the first dataset in which every specification is backed by a checkable certificate of strength or weakness. These labels disagree with the benchmarks' original labels for 16.3% of the methods. These findings highlight the importance of supporting specification strength labels with independently checkable evidence.
item.dc:creator: \'Alvaro Silva, Isabel Amaral, Ruben Martins, Alexandra Mendes

item.title: Does Confusing Code Confuse LLMs? A Pilot Study on C++
item.description: arXiv:2611.15575v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for software maintenance tasks that depend heavily on code comprehension. While atoms of confusion, minimal code patterns empirically shown to impair human program comprehension, are well studied, it remains unclear whether these same patterns affect LLMs, and whether their impact varies across maintenance tasks. We present a pilot study evaluating the impact of atoms of confusion on LLM performance on C++ code drawn from three production libraries, using ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot on three software development tasks: atom injection and removal, output prediction, and code explanation. Our results reveal three preliminary findings: (i) the impact of atoms on LLMs is strongly task-dependent; (ii) atoms requiring reasoning about surrounding code are the most resistant to transformation, while localized syntactic atoms are handled reliably; and (iii) LLMs remove atoms of confusion more reliably than they inject them, suggesting that removal succeeds through pattern matching while injection requires deeper comprehension.
item.dc:creator: Tim van de Wetering, Lola Solovyeva, Fernando Castor

item.title: Bug Finding With Agentic Symbolic Execution
item.description: arXiv:2611.15596v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Symbolic execution, in tools such as CrossHair for Python, is a powerful technique for finding bugs, but two barriers hinder its adoption: the human effort of annotating code with assertions, and the need to model the execution environment outside Python, such as an external database. To overcome both, we design an agentic harness that orchestrates the symbolic execution tool CrossHair together with an AI coding agent. Without human intervention, it instruments a repository with assertions, synthesizes a constraint-aware symbolic environment for the database, runs symbolic execution, and constructs a concrete test as evidence for each bug it reports. We evaluate our harness on 1,156,044 lines of Python code over 11 popular open-source Python web applications (Zulip, NetBox, Apache Superset, and others). With the synthesized environment, CrossHair executes 81% of the 5,406 contracted functions, against 4.5% without it. Our pipeline finds 1,050 bugs, each reproduced by a test against the unmodified application, 221 of them by CrossHair, and 312 of them are missed by a baseline in which the same LLM inspects the code. The two find different kinds of bugs: CrossHair's are mostly crashes on input-domain corner cases that validation admits, such as empty strings, missing fields and unusual characters, while inspection's are mostly bugs that produce wrong output. Our framework thus lets symbolic execution supplement inspection-based bug finding.
item.dc:creator: George Granberry, Wolfgang Ahrendt, Andy Gordon, Moa Johansson

item.title: When Agents Need to Consolidate Memories: What RRR Consolidation Explains, and What It Does Not Explain, in Conversation ESAA
item.description: arXiv:2611.15644v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language-model agents can share conversational history across sessions, but persistence does not guarantee retrieval of current decisions and their provenance. This engineering study presents Memory-TCG, a Conversation ESAA extension inspired by ringing, resonance and renormalization (RRR), and an exploratory synthetic evaluation comparing chronological retrieval, two simplified baselines (B, recency-aware, and B', authority-aware), full RRR, and variants under three output budgets. With 480 facts and 1,024 tokens, full RRR recalled 0.44 of current decisions, versus 0.06 for chronological retrieval and 0.58 for the oracle ceiling; with 4,096 tokens it recalled all of them. B' and the no-resonance variant matched full RRR in decision recall across all nine scale-budget combinations, as expected when the active decision set and the adapter ordering are the same. The isolated contribution of ringing to decisions was not measured: comparator D1 cuts facts before the graph is built, and the product retains active decisions by rule. Before the output limit, full-RRR conflict F1 was 0.615 at all three scales; after it, at 480 facts and 1,024 tokens, it was 0.000. Reserving 20% of the budget for conflicts raised that F1 to 0.431 in that scenario, at the cost of lowering decision recall from 0.44 to 0.34, and to 0.930 at 4,096 tokens without decision loss. Fixtures are repetitive, comparators are simplified, and the evaluation was not independently replicated; the results support an engineering analysis, not a claim of selectionist superiority.
item.dc:creator: Elzo Brito dos Santos Filho

item.title: AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System for Intelligent HPC User Support
item.description: arXiv:2611.15700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI-based question-answering systems are increasingly used for user support, including at high-performance computing (HPC) facilities. However, existing systems lack a systematic, deployment-oriented approach for evaluating final-answer quality and attributing failures to specific components. They also remain largely static after deployment, apart from periodic knowledge-base updates. We present AskALCF, an agentic log-analysis and improvement pipeline for HPC user support. AskALCF evaluates production interactions at a fine-grained level, identifies whether failures arise from missing knowledge, retrieval, prompting, model behavior, or tool execution, and routes each failure to an actionable repair. Its diagnostic core combines answer-quality assessment with a two-scope sufficiency test that distinguishes information missing from the documentation corpus from information present but not retrieved. We further introduce a controlled harness-training process that uses expert references, null edits, and explicit ship, revert, or decline decisions to improve the diagnostic pipeline reliably. Across 2,174 support turns, AskALCF reduced unattributable failures from 41.4% to 14.2%, while harness training improved expert agreement from 108/150 to 123/150 turns. These results demonstrate a governed form of self-evolution in which production evidence drives targeted system improvements. By turning production interactions into fine-grained diagnoses and actionable repairs, AskALCF provides a systematic foundation for continuously improving deployed AI support systems beyond knowledge-base updates alone.
item.dc:creator: Jingyan Jiang, Akhilesh Bondapalli, Krishna Rauniyar, Murat Keceli, Yasaman Ghadar, Haritha Siddabathuni Som, Venkatram Vishwanath, Michael E. Papka, Rong Ge, Huihuo Zheng

item.title: Early Reflections on How Large Language Models are Reshaping Software Engineering Research
item.description: arXiv:2611.15797v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are radically reshaping software engineering (SE) research. Yet, their steep financial and computational costs raise questions about who participates in that change, and who does not. By analysing all 1,918 papers published in the ICSE 2019-2026 Research and SEIP tracks, we uncover a shifting and highly concentrated research landscape. China and the US dominate LLM-based SE research, appearing in 74% of LLM-based publications between 2023-2026, yet they diverge sharply in their use of commercial versus open-weight models. Beneath this national dominance lies extreme institutional concentration: just 5 institutions in China and 7 in the US appear in more than half of their respective nations' LLM-based output. In the US, only half of the unique institutions active in 2023-2026 participated in LLM-based research, whereas Singapore displays broader usage, with 11 of 15 active institutions participating in LLM-based work. Furthermore, across 2023-2026 Research-track papers, industry involvement is more prevalent in LLM-based work (23.4% vs 16.9%), and academia-only papers make up a smaller share (63.4% vs 70.9%). Crucially, we expose a gap in model usage across industry and academia. SEIP track papers lean strongly towards commercial LLMs, with 77.4% featuring them and 40.5% using them exclusively. In contrast, only 21.2% of Research-track work relies strictly on commercial models, making greater use of open-weight models that typically support more sustainable and reproducible experiments. However, this divide warrants reflection on the extent to which SE research aligns with industry practice.
item.dc:creator: David Williams, Michail Kyrkos, Max Hort, Maria Kechagia, Justyna Petke, Federica Sarro

item.title: Spec-Driven PBT: Deriving Semantic Invariants from Code Specifications for Agentic Property-based Testing
item.description: arXiv:2611.15920v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Software is increasingly written by AI agents that produce an implementation from a natural language specification, a practice known as agentic coding. Code is now produced faster than it can be reviewed, and has been shown to exhibit its own characteristic failure patterns. Property-based testing (PBT), a long-standing technique in which invariant properties of a program are checked against many generated inputs, has recently been revisited with LLM agents authoring the properties, thereby removing the high-effort derivation of invariants that has long hindered its adoption. Existing methods, however, derive these properties from the implementation alone (Code-driven PBT). At the same time, a thorough specification such as a product requirements document has become routine within agentic coding, yet its role in testing the resulting code remains underexplored. We study the value of the specification as a source of properties for testing agent-written code. Our key insight is that the specification, unlike the implementation, records what the code was meant to do, and invariants derived from it are not biased by particular implementation choices. We propose Spec-Driven PBT, an agent that first expresses invariants in natural language from the specification and only then inspects the implementation to translate them into concrete tests. Across 25 applications from ViBench, Spec-Driven PBT finds a novel set of bugs that Code-driven PBT misses, while writing 2.4x fewer property tests. Though the two approaches surface a roughly equivalent number of bugs, there is little overlap: nearly 60% of the 169 total bugs are found by only one. Qualitatively, we find that the bugs unique to Spec-Driven PBT tend to violate documented product workflows whereas those to Code-driven PBT instead concentrate on implementation robustness, offering complementary value for bug discovery in agent-written code.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Shukla, Kartik Gupta, Ali Alavi, Pashootan Vaezipoor

item.title: ADAPT: Agentic Diff-Aware Patch Testing for Pull Requests
item.description: arXiv:2611.16114v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern software development relies on pull requests (PRs) that introduce small, targeted code changes. Once merged, these changes should be protected by focused tests that exercise the behavior the PR introduces, yet developers often submit PRs without such tests, leaving the new behavior unguarded against future regressions. Most test generation techniques target entire software units and optimize objectives such as code coverage rather than the behavior a change introduces, and prior diff-aware approaches have had limited success in capturing it. We propose ADAPT (Agentic Diff-Aware Patch Testing), a regression test generation approach that uses an autonomous coding agent to produce change-focused tests for PRs. Given a PR, the agent analyzes the diff between the base and head versions to identify the modified functions and their context, then plans and generates candidate unit tests. A dedicated fail-to-pass (F2P) verification tool runs each candidate on both versions and, after F2P success, reports which executable changed lines remain uncovered; guided by this feedback, the agent iteratively refines its tests. We evaluate ADAPT on the same 426 real-world PRs used by the prior state-of-the-art baseline, with GPT-4o and GPT-5-mini. ADAPT+GPT-4o reaches an F2P rate of 62.0% (264/426), compared with BLAST's reported 35.4% (151/426), while ADAPT+GPT-5-mini reaches 89.9% (383/426). On 137 PRs shared with Change And Cover (ChaCo), ADAPT achieves full patch coverage on 83.9% of PRs, compared with 79.6% for ChaCo, at considerably lower time and cost. A manual evaluation confirms that the F2P-valid tests target each PR's intended change, with mean scores of up to 4.54/5 for importance, 4.35/5 for assertion strength, and 4.49/5 for readability, often covering behavior beyond the developer-written tests.
item.dc:creator: Vahid Haratian, Atakan Akar, Eray T\"uz\"un

item.title: Robo-SWE: An Executable Issue-Resolution Dataset Mined from Robot Software Repositories
item.description: arXiv:2611.16116v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents are evaluated mostly on general-purpose software, but domain-specific systems require domain-aware evaluation. Robot software is a particularly challenging case: Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) packages have their own build tools, simulators and learning frameworks are built on physics engines, and behavior that depends on timing and hardware is hard to test. We present Robo-SWE, a dataset of 236 executable issue-resolution tasks mined from merged pull requests in 28 public robotics repositories in four domains: ROS 2 systems, simulation and physics engines, robotics algorithm libraries, and robot-learning frameworks. Each task contains the original issue text, a container recipe for the repository at the commit before the fix, the developers' fix, and the developers' tests, which fail before the fix and pass after it in repeated offline runs. The dataset also keeps a provenance ledger of all 1,567 candidate pull requests, with the stage each reached and the reason for every rejection, and, as a first use, 3,540 graded attempts by five coding-agent setups with recorded patches and 3,529 available trajectories. Across three runs per primary setup, resolve rates range from 45.8% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 to 56.5% for Claude Opus 5.5; GPT-6.1 Sol reaches 54.1% at maximum effort and 52.5% at medium effort, and GPT-6 Astra 51.4%. GLM-5.3 resolves 46.2%, and Kimi K3.1 Pro 43.9%. The tasks are validated by execution; verification of their fairness by human reviewers is future work. The dataset and public leaderboard are available online.
item.dc:creator: Vahid Haratian, Vahid Ansari, Mohammadhossein Malmir, Alois Knoll

item.title: Guided Generation of Linux Kernel Semantic Patches with Small Local Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.16215v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a Linux kernel API changes, hundreds of drivers are converted by hand over months, and the earlier conversions are reviewed examples for the later ones. We ask whether small open language models running on a laptop can turn such examples into Coccinelle semantic patches, the rules kernel maintainers already use for tree-wide changes. We adapt guided code generation to this task: the training examples are decomposed by script into a tree of change variants, the model writes one small rule per variant under feedback from applying it to the examples, deterministic components repair SmPL syntax and generalise driver-specific names, rules are composed greedily, and a compile critic repairs or rejects a rule whose output does not build. We evaluate on a pre-registered test set of 7 migrations whose new APIs appeared after the training cutoffs of all three models (Qwen2.5-Coder 7B, Llama 3.1 8B, Gemma 3 4B), with 122 held-out driver conversions, counting a conversion as solved only if the rule's output matches the human fix and compiles. With the framework, Qwen2.5-Coder solves 35.3 conversions on average over three seeds (range 32-41), against 1.0 when prompted directly; Spinfer solves 41 and a frontier LLM agent 66. The local model solves fewer conversions than Spinfer but its rules are the most precise on the test set (0.74 of the files they change are solved, against 0.55 for Spinfer and 0.70 for the frontier agent), and the compile critic removes every output that matches the human fix but does not build. The two general-purpose models stay weak even with guidance (at most 12 solved). All code, prompts, model responses and results are released.
item.dc:creator: Mohanned Ahmed

item.title: Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.16289v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents often fail to meet all requirements in the task description. In some of these failures, the agent considers an implementation choice that meets a requirement, but later decides to commit to another one that does not meet the requirement for a reason it finds acceptable. We call this specification satisficing. It is challenging to identify and mitigate specification satisficing because the agent accepts such choices for its own reasons, and existing self-correction methods are biased toward them. We propose SatisFix, which guides a coding agent to report these choices and their reasons, and then check each choice against the task description. We evaluate SatisFix on DeepSWE and SWE-bench Pro with five LLMs as backbones and two different agent frameworks, and compare it with three self-correction methods. SatisFix improves the pass@1 of the base agent by an average of 5.09% on DeepSWE and 7.06% on the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro. On DeepSWE, it outperforms the best baseline by 3.98%. Our ablation study shows that both steps of SatisFix contribute to the improvement.
item.dc:creator: Ruixin Wang, Tianyi Zhang

item.title: Rasoi: Visual Diffs for Evaluating Structural Changes Made by Coding Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.16293v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents let developers modify software rapidly through natural language. However, as agents take on larger changes, developers can lose track of how the codebase is evolving. These edits may look correct on the surface while restructuring the system in unexpected ways: duplicating logic, changing modules outside the requested scope, removing functionality developers meant to keep, or introducing architectural drift. We investigate how visual diffs can help developers understand and evaluate the structural changes that coding agents make. We present Rasoi, a design probe that maps how a codebase's architecture evolves after each agent-made edit, letting developers inspect which architectural elements and relationships were added, modified, or removed across multiple levels of abstraction. We deployed Rasoi in a week-long study with 12 developers working on their own codebases across varied technical domains. We found that visual diffs helped developers see whether changes stayed within scope, notice unexpected restructuring, and understand how modified parts related to the system as a whole. Our findings suggest that the value of oversight tools for coding agents lies less in making developers trust the agent and more in helping developers feel confident in their own evaluation of agent-made changes. We discuss implications for visual tools that support code comprehension and human oversight in AI-assisted software development.
item.dc:creator: Riya Sahni, Aryan Kaul, Anushka Bhatnagar, Xuanming Zhang, Vivian Liu, Reya Vir, Lydia B. Chilton

item.title: Non-Functional Requirements to Hyperparameter Translation for Quantum Software via LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2611.16902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum software engineering (QSE) lacks validated approaches for translating natural-language non-functional requirements (NFRs) into execution parameters such as shots and transpiler optimization levels. Existing methods emphasize semantic similarity rather than execution outcomes. We evaluate seven large language models (LLMs) against a deterministic heuristic baseline using 540 synthetic and 18 real-world user stories. We assess semantic accuracy and execution outcomes, including time, cost, top-state probability, and two-qubit gate exposure, through Qiskit/Aer simulations. All LLMs significantly outperformed the heuristic in semantic accuracy, achieving 55.6 to 83.3 percent on real-world stories compared to 16.7 percent for the heuristic. However, no LLM demonstrated statistically significant superiority over others on the real-world dataset. Speed- and cost-oriented configurations reduced execution time and cost, but fidelity improvements were not supported. Some failures resulted from provider safety refusals rather than translation errors. Our findings demonstrate the potential of LLMs as middleware for NFR-to-configuration translation in QSE, while emphasizing execution-based validation, human oversight, and careful interpretation of model differences.
item.dc:creator: Joseph G. Bronyah, Nasir U. Eisty

item.title: Patterns for Designing CI/CD Workflows
item.description: arXiv:2611.17276v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: CI/CD pipelines are difficult to build and maintain, and information about them is scattered across empirical studies, practitioner books, and catalogues of 'smells'. We collected candidate practices and anti-practices converted them into patterns, and then consolidated these into patterns. These patterns address issues such as security, pipeline scheduling, workflow structure, performance and failure and release management. Each pattern is contextualised and describes the problem it solves, the forces at play, the solution and the consequences.
item.dc:creator: Leandro Sousa, Filipe Correia

item.title: Where LLM Agents Get Stuck Debugging Databases: Access More Than Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2611.17304v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents are increasingly asked not only to write code but to debug running systems from live runtime data. We report a field observation of one such agent (Claude Code) as it diagnosed eight database incidents in a production message-dispatch engine. In every incident whose root cause depended on runtime concurrency, the agent announced a cause, shipped a fix, and later walked it back, and each wrong guess cost a deploy-and-observe cycle. Mapping each incident to what the agent lacked, we find that access to production state was the most pervasive bottleneck. The missing access included live lock views, untruncated deadlock reports, read-only execution, and an explicit environment context. An access gap was present in all five concurrency-dependent incidents: alone in one, and in four combined with a reasoning error such as anchoring on an early cause, incomplete exploration of the configuration, or a misreading of the code's transaction semantics. The three incidents that did not depend on concurrency needed nothing beyond what the agent already had. Within the incidents, the agent's wrong hypotheses were consistent with the evidence it could see; they were not fabrications. We argue that the next step for production-debugging agents is a forensics layer that gives the agent the access it lacks inside existing security controls. Such a layer would combine a safe interrogation API, a lock-and-deadlock flight recorder, and a production replay harness.
item.dc:creator: Gustavo Pinto

item.title: OverServe: Resource Amplification Attacks on SaaS Agents via Tool--Prompt Co-Design
item.description: arXiv:2611.14808v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are enabling software-as-a-service (SaaS) providers to automate longer business workflows with agents. In subscription-based SaaS deployments, model and tool calls consume provider resources without additional customer payments. Because the agent autonomously decides when to stop, a malicious tenant can send a prompt to the agent, exploiting its completion decisions to extend execution and waste provider resources. In this paper, we present OverServe, a multi-agent framework for constructing such attacks against SaaS agents. OverServe co-designs Model Context Protocol (MCP) status tools and completion-confirmation prompts for the attacker. Each tool call returns accurate status and terminates normally, yet the agent may repeatedly check an unfinished condition to satisfy the prompt. This consumes the SaaS provider's resources even after the original business task is completed. OverServe constructs service-specific tool--prompt pairs and uses separate tool and prompt reviews to guide candidate pair selection. Tested tool specifications trigger no alerts in the evaluated MCP scanners. We evaluate Qwen, Nemotron, DeepSeek, and Sonnet on selected tasks from nine benchmarks. All OverServe runs pass the original task checks. OverServe can reach a maximal amplification of API requests by $93.88\times$ while preserving the original task goal and collateral checks.
item.dc:creator: Ruiheng Yu, Oteo Mamo, Siyu Gan, Weikuan Yu, Mulong Luo

item.title: Towards Runtime-Aware Observability for Java Virtual Threads
item.description: arXiv:2611.14999v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: OS-level observability tools join application requests to kernel events through the OS thread ID, assuming that a unit of work occupies one OS thread until it completes. Java virtual threads break this assumption: many virtual threads are multiplexed onto a few carrier threads, so a stable thread ID hides a changing unit of work, and the join fails silently. Existing virtual-thread-aware channels republish context or identity on every mount and unmount, and the JVMTI-based one pays this cost for the lifetime of the JVM, whether or not an observer is attached. We bind a 64-byte off-heap trace buffer to each virtual thread, at a fixed address for its lifetime, and publish the address to eBPF consumers through four USDT probes in a patched OpenJDK; a re-implemented JVMTI channel over the same buffer serves as a controlled comparison. The four-probe design attributed all 768 test markers correctly on both the content and the identity plane, while the naive two-probe design silently misattributes trace context. With no consumer attached, publication costs at most about 33 ns per transition; the remaining dormant cost is buffer allocation, about 0.37 microseconds per virtual thread, which is negligible on transition-heavy workloads but nearly doubles the cost of a creation-only microbenchmark. The JVMTI channel costs about 20% on transition-heavy workloads and about 1.8 microseconds per virtual thread on the creation-only one. We also show that, of the two update strategies OTEP 4947 permits, only in-place rewriting guarded by the record's valid flag is sound for readers that cache the record's address, as lifecycle-event readers do.
item.dc:creator: Wenjie Ding

item.title: EvoX: Rethinking the Agent Harness as a Runtime Policy
item.description: arXiv:2611.15006v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly interact with tools and environments, yet plausible model decisions do not always translate into successful execution due to tool-call mismatches, interrupted workflows, and unsupported completion claims. We present EvoX, a Rust-based, multi-model agent runtime guided by The Second Policy, which views the harness as an Operational Policy complementing the foundation model's Semantic Policy. EvoX combines model-facing guidance with deterministic runtime control through three complementary mechanisms: Action Realization, Execution Continuity, and Outcome Grounding. To evaluate harnesses without suppressing their native behaviors, we introduce Contrast, a controlled and auditable framework integrating explicit fairness constraints, provider-bound request verification, and evidence-based adjudication. Across five benchmarks, six foundation models, and six agent harnesses, EvoX achieves the highest numerical success rate of 56.2% over 691 common task--model pairs, exceeding the average of the other five harnesses by approximately 3.0 percentage points. Its larger advantages on GLM-5.3 (+10.7 points) and Kimi K3 (+7.9 points) highlight the model-dependent effectiveness of harness design and the potential for cross-provider adaptability. Achieved without memory, evolution, or extensions, these results establish EvoX as a competitive multi-model agent runtime and underscore the importance of harness-level operational control in realizing foundation-model capabilities.
item.dc:creator: Haoyang Zhang, Qumeng Sun, Xiao Zhang, Xiang Liu, Zhidong Fan, Junjie Wang

item.title: IoTPwnBench: A Synthetic Benchmark for IoT Firmware Security Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.15316v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Building and evaluating security tools for IoT firmware requires targets whose weaknesses are known in ad- vance and can be reproduced in a running device. Two problems remain: (1) firmware collected from real-world products provides realistic software, but hardware dependencies and undocumented defects make it difficult to establish what a security tool should be expected to find; and (2) existing benchmarks typically collect sets of vulnerable or misconfigured firmware images without providing purpose-built vulnerable services with explicit weaknesses that a security analysis tool can target. We present IoTPwnBench, a synthetic, modular benchmark that brings these requirements together. IoTPwnBench contains 716 vulnerable firmware images covering 86 weakness scenarios and 28 CWE classes across 11 device profiles, including industrial controllers, health monitors, and household devices. Each vulnerable image runs a plausible device application with simulated sensors and actuators that generate live readings over its native interfaces while exposing one target weakness mapped to a primary CWE. A documented exploitation payload and observable signal establish the expected behavior independently of the evaluated tool. Every vulnerable image is paired with a corrected twin that preserves the device and service while removing that weakness. Researchers can therefore compare the same target before and after correction to assess detection and false positives for the target weakness. The benchmark produces kernel and filesystem binaries for static inspection and dynamic testing under QEMU. Device profiles and weakness modules remain separate, allowing the same scenario to be reused across device contexts. Vulnerable targets were validated manually, and the open source build workflow regenerates the firmware bit-for-bit.
item.dc:creator: Luca Ferrari, Marco Alecci, Luca Verderame, Jacques Klein, Francesco Pagano

item.title: Orbit: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on IT Operations Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2611.15718v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLMs now support IT operations (ITOps), but benchmarks rarely show why a model fails. We present ORBIT, a benchmark of ITOps questions in three formats, namely multiple-choice, open-ended, and troubleshooting, with each question accompanied by a reference answer and a recorded source. An audit found template defects in about a tenth of the generated items, so we drop them and rebuild the troubleshooting format from real practitioner threads with accepted answers. Under one independent judge, five LLMs answer most multiple-choice items correctly, between a third and just over half of the open-ended items, and a minority of the troubleshooting items, even under a more lenient root-cause rubric. When models judged their own answers, they accepted many answers to defective items, so we use one independent judge for every model. Word overlap with the question finds the correct option for more than half of the multiple-choice items. ORBIT is a diagnostic aid for selecting and supervising assistants rather than a deployment test.
item.dc:creator: Sathwik Narkedimilli, Rakshit Verma, Rahul Soni, Ankit Kushwaha, Balaji Ganesan, Kaustabha Ray, Sunil Saumya, Pratibha Moogi

item.title: Beyond the Diff - VulSpot: A Vulnerability Dataset Where No Vulnerability Goes Unlocalized
item.description: arXiv:2611.15737v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A vulnerability detector is only as trustworthy as the benchmark that scores it, and today's real-world datasets tend to flatter detectors. They are often built once and never refreshed, so they quickly miss new vulnerabilities, their labels are either noisy or heavily filtered, and their random splits let models train on near-copies of test code and on future vulnerabilities. Above all, when a fix only adds code, such as a missing NULL check, they do not point at where the vulnerability was, preventing detectors from learning to localize some of the most common C/C++ weaknesses. We present VulSpot, a living benchmark for detecting, classifying, and localizing vulnerabilities, with over 500k functions in 21 languages from 24k registered CVEs, including over 15k vulnerable C/C++ functions. By linking the code added by a patch to the existing statement it protects, VulSpot locates the vulnerability in 99.3\% of the functions that previous diff-based datasets used to leave without a location. Rather than discarding uncertain labels, it tells users how reliable each one is, and it comes with leak-free splits, complementary code context, and hierarchical CWE labels. An automated pipeline refreshes VulSpot every month, so that each release brings vulnerabilities no model has seen yet.
item.dc:creator: Dyna Soumhane Ouchebara, St\'ephane Dupont

item.title: Does a Self-Learning Migration Agent Learn? An Audited Evaluation of Evidence-Graded Experience Memory for Oracle-to-PostgreSQL Migration
item.description: arXiv:2611.16143v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Do large language model (LLM) migration agents learn from accumulated experience, or do apparent gains reflect retrieval and reference reuse? We evaluate an evidence-graded agent for Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration across four studies.
